items.title: Sperry's Nobel work showed hemispheres process independently
items.claim: Roger Sperry's split-brain research (Nobel 1981) found that when the corpus callosum is severed and images shown to only one visual field, what happens?

options.text: Both hemispheres still share all information
An object shown only to the left visual field (right hemisphere) cannot be named verbally (because language is typically left-hemisphere lateralised) but can be selected by touch with the left hand

items.reveal_title: Hemispheres can act independently after callosotomy
items.reveal:
Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied epilepsy patients who had undergone callosotomy. Their experiments showed each hemisphere could process information without conscious awareness in the other, raising deep questions about the unity of consciousness.

The popular 'left-brain logical, right-brain creative' caricature is wildly oversimplified — both hemispheres contribute to most cognitive tasks in intact brains. Lateralisation is real but localised to specific functions (language, visuospatial processing).
items.why: Findings about rare clinical populations can constrain theories of normal cognition. The popular interpretation often outruns the evidence.

items.title: Gage's personality change was real but exaggerated in retelling
items.claim: The story of Phineas Gage (1848) is widely taught as a sudden, permanent personality transformation. What does modern scholarship suggest?

options.text: He was permanently and severely changed forever

Personality changes occurred but Macmillan (2000) and others find evidence of substantial recovery over time; Gage worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile for years, requiring social and planning skills
Gage was unaffected by the injury

items.reveal:
Malcolm Macmillan's 'An Odd Kind of Fame' (2000) compiled the historical record. After his 1848 accident, Gage worked at a livery stable in New Hampshire, then drove a long-distance stagecoach in Valparaiso, Chile (1852-59) — a demanding job requiring planning, social interaction and route management.

He died in 1860 after a series of seizures. The neuroimaging reconstructions of his injury (Damasio et al. 1994, Van Horn et al. 2012) suggest damage to left frontal regions and white matter tracts.

The textbook story ('No longer Gage') exaggerates permanence.
items.why: Iconic case studies become simplified in retelling. The brain's capacity for functional reorganisation matters for both clinical practice and theory.

items.title: HM could form new procedural but not episodic memories
items.claim: Henry Molaison (HM) had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 for severe epilepsy. After the operation:

options.text: He had no memory of any kind
He could not form new conscious (declarative) memories but could acquire procedural skills like mirror-tracing — improving with practice while denying ever having done the task
He recovered fully within a year
He became a famous psychologist himself

items.reveal:
Brenda Milner began studying HM in 1955. Her 1962 paper documented procedural learning despite dense anterograde amnesia. HM died in 2008; his identity was revealed posthumously. His brain was sliced into 2,401 sections (Annese et al. 2014) and photographed, available online.

His case established that medial temporal lobe (especially hippocampus) is essential for new declarative memory formation but not for procedural learning. Suzanne Corkin worked with HM for 46 years.
items.why: Single-case neuropsychology can produce findings that constrain theories of normal cognition for generations. The dissociation between memory systems was visible in one patient.
